subtype: Approach: seeks a teacher when stuck after trying alone [Thinking]
passage:
Abhinav here. I sit behind Manjula, so I saw everything. The problem said a rope is 12 metres long and is cut into pieces of 3 metres. How many pieces? Manjula worked on it for ten minutes, biting her pencil. Then she picked up her notebook and walked to the teacher's desk.

"I tried, Ma'am. I did 12 minus 3 and got 9. But 9 doesn't sound like pieces."

The teacher looked at her page. "What does 9 tell you?"

"It's the rope left after one cut. I have to keep cutting... oh! It's 12 shared into 3s." She wrote 4 and smiled. I don't know if she felt silly or happy, but she ran back to her seat fast.

qa.q: What answer did Manjula get when she did 12 minus 3?
How was Manjula feeling about her answer of 9, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Manjula felt doubtful and unsure, since she said 9 did not sound like pieces, so she wanted help finding the mistake.

qa.q: What could Manjula try next time she is stuck?
qa.a: Manjula could draw the rope cut into pieces first, and bring her attempt to the teacher if she is still stuck.

qa.q: Why can Abhinav only guess how Manjula felt at the end?
qa.a: Abhinav sat behind and saw only the smile and the quick run back, so cannot know Manjula's feelings for sure.

grounding: Shows a girl trying a maths problem alone and then showing the teacher her attempt so the mistake in her thinking can be seen.

subtype: Approach: seeks a teacher when stuck after trying alone [Thinking]
passage:
Monday: Avni spent twenty minutes on question 7, the one about two trains leaving from different stations. She tried drawing the tracks, rubbed it out, tried a table. Her eraser left a hole in the page. "Okay," she whispered. "I've tried three ways. Now I need someone to see what I did, not just give me the answer."

Tuesday: Before assembly she took her messy page to Reena Ma'am. "I think I went wrong somewhere here," Avni said, pointing. "I added their speeds, but maybe I should have subtracted?" Reena Ma'am smiled. "What made you unsure?" Avni thought. "They're going the same way, so they're not coming closer fast."

Thursday: In the quiz, a similar question came up. Avni didn't panic. She drew the arrows first.

qa.q: Which question did Avni spend twenty minutes on?
qa.a: Question 7, the one about two trains leaving from different stations.

qa.q: How did Avni feel on Thursday when a similar question came up?
qa.a: She felt calm and confident; she didn't panic because she now understood why the direction of the trains mattered.

qa.q: Why did bringing her messy page to Reena Ma'am work well?
qa.a: Reena Ma'am could see exactly where Avni's thinking went wrong and ask a question, so Avni found the fix herself.

qa.q: What would change if Avni had only asked for the answer?
qa.a: She might have copied it without knowing why, and the Thursday quiz question could have caught her out again.

grounding: A girl works a maths problem alone, then brings her attempt to the teacher so the teacher can see where her thinking went wrong.

subtype: Approach: seeks a teacher when stuck after trying alone [Thinking]
passage: Shreya, you think I was always good at sums? No. When I was a girl of eleven, there was a problem about filling a tank with two taps. I sat with it for a whole evening. I tried one way, then another. My pages were full of crossings. My brother said, "Just ask Master-ji for the answer." But I thought, if I only get the answer, I will be stuck again next week. So I took my crossed-out pages to school. I told Master-ji, "This is how I thought. Somewhere it breaks." He read my pages and put his finger on one line. "Here, you forgot one tap was emptying." I nearly laughed. The next tank problem, I solved alone. That's how your Pooja Nani learnt.

qa.q: What was the problem young Pooja struggled with?
qa.a: A problem about filling a tank with two taps.

qa.q: Why did young Pooja refuse to just ask for the answer?
qa.a: She was worried that with only the answer she would be stuck again next week; she wanted to understand where her own thinking broke.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Taking her crossed-out pages to Master-ji; seeing her working let him point to the exact line where she forgot one tap was emptying.

qa.q: How might Master-ji have felt reading her pages?
qa.a: He was probably pleased and impressed to see a student who had really tried, which made it easy for him to help quickly.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a girl, trying a maths problem for an evening and taking her own attempt to the teacher to find the flaw.
